rows.statement: The 'some' line of a memory pressure file is the share of time in which at least some tasks are stalled on that resource; the 'full' line is the share of time in which all non-idle tasks are stalled simultaneously. systemd-oomd's memory-pressure limit is documented as the share of time in a 10 second window in which all tasks of the control group were delayed, which is the 'full' line of that cgroup's memory pressure file [inference from oomd.conf(5) and the kernel's definition of 'full']. A rising 'some' value with a much lower 'full' value is therefore partial stall and never by itself an oomd condition.
rows.action: Read 'full' and 'some' together before quoting either, and quote the 'full' share when the question is 'would systemd-oomd have acted'. Do not read a high lifetime full/some ratio as thrashing on its own: the ratio here is 40856373 / 41385384 = 0.987 lifetime while the current averages are at or below 0.06 percent.

quotes.quote: line indicates the share of time in which at least some tasks are stalled on a given resource.

rows.statement: The 'total' field of a memory pressure line is absolute stall time in microseconds, accumulated monotonically inside one boot. A single read never dates an incident: a dated reading needs two reads of the same file in the same boot and the difference between them. systemd-oomd's own rule is not a difference of totals; it is a sustained-limit rule, so a stall that ends inside the 30 second default duration never reaches the oomd action even though a difference of totals would show it.
rows.action: Take two reads with a known gap and subtract, and record the boot identity with the pair. In this capture the gap was the 'sleep 10' of capture line 17: some 41389485 - 41385384 = 4101 us and full 40860452 - 40856373 = 4079 us, that is 0.041 percent of the interval. A zero difference is not proof of no stall.

rows.statement: Every cgroup directory exposes memory.pressure in the same format as /proc/pressure/. The root cgroup's file is not a summary of its children: the kernel maps the root cgroup onto the system pressure group, so the root file prints the system group's counters and equals /proc/pressure/memory by identity. A system-scope read therefore says nothing about any non-root cgroup, and a parent total is not the sum of its children. systemd-oomd watches the memory.pressure file of the cgroups it monitors, not /proc/pressure/memory.
rows.action: Name the cgroup whose pressure is being read before quoting it, and never compare a parent total with a child total taken from sequential reads: time passes between the reads, and a child can legitimately exceed its parent. In this capture the sequential reads give user.slice 3150158 us, user-1000.slice 3158801 us and user@1000.service 3161820 us of some total, which is a time artifact, not a hierarchy.

rows.statement: ManagedOOMMemoryPressure= and ManagedOOMSwap= decide whether systemd-oomd may act on a unit's cgroup. 'kill' makes the unit a candidate for monitoring and adds After= and Wants= dependencies on systemd-oomd.service. 'auto' is the default and means systemd-oomd will not actively use that cgroup's data for monitoring and detection; an 'auto' unit becomes a kill candidate only when an ancestor cgroup is set to 'kill'. systemd-oomd monitors only cgroups whose units carry 'kill'. On this host systemd-oomd is inactive and disabled, and every one of the four captured units (user@1000.service, user-1000.slice, user.slice and -.slice) carries 'auto' on both properties, so the whole ancestor chain up to the root slice is 'auto' and nothing in it is monitored.
rows.action: Read the two properties on a unit before assuming any protection from systemd-oomd. Enabling the unit would still monitor nothing while every unit stays 'auto'; setting 'kill' on a unit, or enabling systemd-oomd, is an operator action outside this lane, and the operator must check for the running userspace killer (earlyoom is active and enabled on this host) before deciding what a second killer would do. Do not read MemoryPressureWatch= as an oomd property: it is the service-side pressure export with no kill semantics.

rows.statement: For the installed systemd 262 the systemd-oomd defaults are a memory-pressure limit of 60 percent, a memory-pressure duration of 30 seconds and a swap-use limit of 90 percent. The swap rule fires only when the fraction of memory used and the fraction of swap used are both above the limit, and only on descendant cgroups holding more than 5 percent of total swap. A unit's ManagedOOMMemoryPressureLimit=0 means 'use the default', and it is ignored unless that unit is 'kill'. This host's /etc/systemd/oomd.conf sets no local key, so the shipped defaults are the effective ones.
rows.action: Read the three commented keys as the effective defaults for this host. Never read the 90 percent rule as a swap-only rule, and never read ManagedOOMMemoryPressureLimit=0 as a zero-percent limit. On this host at capture time memory used was 24.77 percent and swap used 5.41 percent, so neither arm of the swap conjunction was near its limit.

rows.statement: The kernel raises its OOM-kill counters in the kill path, in a different file from the one where stall time is accumulated. A cgroup's memory.events oom_kill field counts the processes of that cgroup killed by any kind of OOM killer, while the PSI total counts stall time. A userspace killer's SIGKILL moves neither counter, so the kernel counter reads zero even when a userspace killer has killed something.
rows.action: Read the kernel counter and the stall counter separately, and never read one as the other. This capture never read earlyoom, so no claim is made that nothing watches memory before the kernel: the supplementary read-only capture shows earlyoom.service active and enabled on this host, and an earlyoom kill would not move the kernel counters. A zero oom_kill is a statement about one counter in one scope since one boot, never about the absence of memory-related kills.
